score_notes.novelty: Duchamp’s Rotoreliefs are a fresh found object for this catalogue, while the CSS scroll timeline supplies a new mechanism in which the reader’s scrollbar becomes the disc’s motor.
score_notes.nuance: The scroll-bound rotation makes motion dependency and the flat readymade one mechanism, but the fixed HUD, fallback prose, and cartel state the optical and art-historical readings instead of leaving a self-sufficient double code.
score_notes.narrative: Replacing Duchamp’s turntable with the reader’s scroll directly answers Rotoreliefs, differentiates the continuous CSS timeline from y-a-v-a’s Sallie Gardner at a Gallop, and makes deterministic order materially legible.
score_notes.craft: The sticky scroll timeline and one-time geometry generation are compact, but the duplicated opaque fallback overlays apologize for missing support and hide the promised still print, leaving the build less disciplined than its core.
score_notes.wit: The dry claim that the disc turns because the document is long lands cleanly as the motor-and-dependency gag, but it is mostly delivered once rather than opening a second comic reading on revisit.

references_named: y-a-v-a, Sallie Gardner at a Gallop (2026)
rationale: All hard gates pass because the work is a live, browser-native canonical remix with a clear argument, compliant licensing and attribution, and no catalogue duplicate. Binding the Rotorelief to the reader’s scroll gives it a strong new mechanism and a precise answer to Duchamp’s dependence of image on motion. The explanatory overlays and defective fallback states blunt its nuance and craft.
reservations: The unsupported and reduced-motion branches cover the disc with opaque explanatory panels, so the claimed still-print state is never actually seen; the fixed HUD and cartel also explain the double reading that the motion could carry unaided.
revision_suggestion: Keep the disc visible in both fallback states while presenting the notices around or beneath it, and trim the fixed explanatory prose so the scroll-driven mechanism carries more of the optical and art-historical argument.
